prompt: A metric says 3% of bookings failed in the last five minutes. What can that metric not tell you?
hint: It was aggregated before it was stored.

choices.text: Which bookings they were
choices.why: Right. A count of a million costs the same as a count of ten because the individual events are gone; the log keeps them.

choices.text: Whether the share of failures is going up or down
choices.why: It can: compare the same number over time, which is what a time series is for.

choices.text: How many bookings were attempted in that time
choices.why: It can: that is the rate, the R of RED.

choices.text: How long the bookings took, as a percentile
choices.why: A duration histogram answers that, within the width of a bucket.

prompt: Match each letter of RED and USE to what it measures.
hint: RED looks at a service from its caller's side; USE looks at a resource.

pairs.right: how much work is queued waiting for it

right_distractors: how much each request cost the company

prompt: boxoffice's machine sits at 40% CPU while bookings queue behind booking_lock. What does a USE check that looks only at the hardware report?

choices.text: A saturated processor, from the queue of bookings
choices.why: The queue is on the lock, not on the processors; at 40% the processors are not saturated.

choices.text: A healthy machine, with spare capacity
choices.why: Right, and it is wrong. The lock is a resource too, saturated while the processors idle; USE has to be applied to it.

choices.text: A high error rate on the booking route
choices.why: Errors in RED are failed requests; queued bookings still succeed, slowly.

choices.text: Nothing, since USE only applies to disks and networks
choices.why: USE applies to processors and memory too, and to anything work waits for.

prompt: Why does observed.py send the request id back to the client in a header, and not only write it into the log?
hint: Who needs to quote it later?

choices.text: Prometheus reads the header to count requests
choices.why: Prometheus reads /metrics and never sees a response to a customer.

choices.text: The browser needs it to keep the session open
choices.why: Sessions are a cookie's job; the id identifies one request, not a user.

choices.text: So a caller quotes it and the one log line is found
choices.why: Right. A complaint, a ticket or a failed synthetic check that carries the id leads straight to its line among millions.

choices.text: HTTP/1.1 requires an id on every response
choices.why: No HTTP version requires one; X-Request-Id is a convention.

prompt: A checkout crosses twenty services and is slow. Which signal shows that the time went in the fourth one?

choices.text: The request counter of the first service
choices.why: A count says how many, and nothing about where the time went.

choices.text: The processor utilisation of every host
choices.why: A slow service may be waiting on something with its processor idle.

choices.text: The log of the last service in the chain
choices.why: It knows its own time; without a shared id it cannot place itself among the other nineteen.

choices.text: A trace
choices.why: Right. Each service adds a span with its duration, and the long one stands out.

prompt: Match each product to the job it started with.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

pairs.right: an agent inside the application timing each transaction
graphs drawn over data stored elsewhere
searching log lines indexed in Elasticsearch
exceptions grouped with their stack traces
metrics from an agent on every host

right_distractors: generating load against a staging server

prompt: A colleague says "our metrics are in Grafana". What is the more exact statement?
hint: What does Grafana store by itself?

choices.text: Grafana draws them from a source such as Prometheus
choices.why: Right. Prometheus, Loki, a SQL database: the data lives there, and Grafana draws the answers.

choices.text: They are in Grafana's own time-series database
choices.why: Grafana stores dashboards, not the series; it queries a data source.

choices.text: They are in the k6 results, which Grafana Labs owns and keeps
choices.why: Grafana Labs owns k6, but k6 is a load generator, not where production metrics live.

choices.text: They are in the application's own log file
choices.why: A log is a different signal; a metrics dashboard does not read raw log lines.

prompt: A team moves from one vendor to another and its services already emit OpenTelemetry. What still has to be rewritten?
hint: OpenTelemetry standardises how data is produced and sent.

choices.text: The instrumentation inside each one of the services
choices.why: That is what OpenTelemetry spares them; the collector's destination changes instead.

choices.text: The dashboards and alerts in the old query language
choices.why: Right. An alert written in one vendor's query language does not move to another's.

choices.text: The wire protocol the collector uses to send data onwards
choices.why: OTLP is the standard part; the five products publish ways to take it in.

choices.text: The applications' HTTP endpoints
choices.why: Monitoring does not change what the application serves to its users.

prompt: Why does observed.py label requests with the route /shows/{id} instead of the path /shows/990?
hint: Every distinct set of labels is a series Prometheus stores.

choices.text: Prometheus refuses labels that contain digits
choices.why: Label values may hold any text; the problem is how many distinct ones there are.

choices.text: The show id is personal data and must stay out of metrics
choices.why: A show id identifies a play, not a person; the reason is the number of series.

choices.text: So one endpoint is one series, not one per show
choices.why: Right. A thousand shows would make a thousand series of one endpoint, and a stranger typing ids could make more.

choices.text: So the path can be read back out of the log
choices.why: The log keeps the full path anyway, in its own field.

prompt: Without guarded, what would a request that raises an exception inside app.py leave in the metrics and the log?
hint: Where are the count and the log line written?

choices.text: A 500 in both, written by the HTTP server itself
choices.why: The standard library's server closes the connection; it does not answer 500 on the handler's behalf.

choices.text: A count with status 0, and a line with no status
choices.why: There is no code path that records a status 0; nothing is recorded at all.

choices.text: A line in the log, but no count in the metrics
choices.why: Both are written in the same method, after the answer, so they fail together.

choices.text: Nothing in either, since send was never called
choices.why: Right. The count and the log line are both written in send, so the failure an operator most needs would be invisible.

prompt: In a Prometheus histogram, the bucket that counts every request, however long it took, is labelled le="___".
hint: It is the last bucket, and the largest bound there is.

prompt: The error-ratio query printed nothing at all. What does that mean here?

choices.text: No 5xx has happened, so there is no series to divide
choices.why: Right. With no series on top there is no result; or vector(0) writes the zero in.

choices.text: Prometheus failed to reach boxoffice
choices.why: up said 1 for boxoffice; a failed scrape shows there, not as an empty division.

choices.text: The error ratio was exactly zero
choices.why: A zero prints as 0, as the second query shows; this printed no series.

choices.text: The query had a syntax error, which curl hid
choices.why: A syntax error comes back as an error object, and the same expression worked with or vector(0).

prompt: k6 reported http_req_failed at 3.00% while Prometheus counted no 5xx. Why do they disagree?
hint: Look at what the 67 failures were.

choices.text: Prometheus loses the requests that arrive between two of its scrapes
choices.why: Counters only grow; a scrape reads the total, so nothing between scrapes is lost.

choices.text: k6 counts every 4xx as failed, including the 409 refusals
choices.why: Right. Refusing a seat already sold is correct behaviour; which statuses count as errors is a decision.

choices.text: k6 abandoned the slowest requests once they had taken 40 ms
choices.why: k6's default timeout is far longer, and the log shows 67 answers of 409.

choices.text: The node exporter's errors were added in
choices.why: The query reads only boxoffice_requests_total; the exporter's series are separate.

prompt: 963 requests to /shows/{id} were counted. Counting from the fastest, which request is the 95th percentile, rounded up?
Prometheus put the p95 of /shows/{id} at 58 ms and k6 put the p95 of all requests at 140 ms. A colleague says Prometheus is wrong. What is the best reply?

choices.text: Prometheus is right and k6's numbers include its own overhead, so they can be ignored
choices.why: What the client waited is what a customer feels; it is not overhead to ignore.

choices.text: k6 is right, because a histogram's estimate is always too low
choices.why: The estimate can fall either way inside its bucket; that does not explain a factor of two.

choices.text: Both are right: one route timed in the server, against every route timed at the client
choices.why: Right. Different operations, measured at different places, including about 40 ms spent outside the application.

choices.text: Neither: percentiles from two tools cannot be compared
choices.why: They can, once both measure the same operation at the same place.

prompt: Put in order the path a booking takes from happening to being a number in your terminal.
hint: Prometheus asks; the application only answers.
items: observed.py adds one to a counter
Prometheus scrapes it and stores a point
rate() turns the points into requests per second
promql.sh prints the answer with jq

prompt: Someone adds a label customer to boxoffice_requests_total so that each customer's requests can be counted. What goes wrong?
hint: Think about cardinality, and about what a metric is kept for.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as Prometheus has enough disk to spare
choices.why: The cost is memory and query time per series, and the privacy problem does not shrink with disk.

choices.text: rate() stops working on counters that carry more than one label
choices.why: rate() works on any counter; every label just makes more series for it to compute.

choices.text: The counter turns into a histogram
choices.why: A label does not change a metric's type.

choices.text: One series per customer, and personal data kept for months
choices.why: Right. Fifty thousand customers are fifty thousand series, and an identifier sits in a store nobody cleans. A per-customer question belongs to the log.

prompt: Which of these belong in the structured log line of a booking? Choose every one that does.
hint: What would an investigation need, and what would a leaked log expose?

choices.text: the request id
choices.why: Yes: it joins the line to the complaint and to the trace.

choices.text: the status and the duration in milliseconds
choices.why: Yes: they are what RED counts, kept per event.

choices.text: the customer's card number, to trace payments
choices.why: Never: logs are copied and kept longer than the database. The payment provider holds the card.

choices.text: the route, as a template like /shows/{id}
choices.why: Yes: it lets the line be grouped with the others of its endpoint.

choices.text: the session token, to replay the request
choices.why: No: whoever reads the log could act as that customer.
